problem: Audio-visual navigation methods fuse visual and audio features by simple concatenation, ignoring context. Most also rely on phase-wise training or extra aids (topology graph, sound semantics) and handle only static sound sources; moving-target chasing is under-studied.
motivation: The relative usefulness of vision versus audio changes as the robot moves and the target moves, so a fixed fusion rule is suboptimal. An end-to-end framework with a context-aware fusion module could chase a moving sound source without extra aids.
key_idea: Replace concatenation fusion with a feature self-attention (FSA) module over the concatenated audio and visual features, inside an end-to-end PPO-trained CNN+GRU actor-critic agent that chases a moving sound target.
insight: Context-aware fusion beats concat, element-wise multiplication and mean fusion in nearly all depth+sound settings (Table 1). The gains are largest in the multiple heard and unheard sound splits and on Matterport3D. Depth is the best visual modality. Heavier encoders (ViT, Capsule) hurt, which the authors attribute to harder convergence. FSA is slightly worse than concat in the blind case (Table 2), suggesting its added flexibility only pays off when visual features are informative. Perturbation-based impact scores show that the modality weighting varies over an episode.
method: Encoders: separate visual (RGB/depth 128x128) and audio (binaural spectrogram) CNNs, each Conv8x8, Conv4x4, Conv3x3 and a 512-d linear layer with ReLU.
FSA fusion: the concatenated feature e_i is used as Q=K=V; e_o = softmax(sigmoid(W1 Q) sigmoid(W2 K)^T / sqrt(d)) V ⊕ V, with d=256, giving a fused embedding.
Temporal module: a bidirectional GRU (512 hidden) turns the fused embeddings into a state s_t.
Actor-critic: single linear layers for the policy and value; actions are MoveForward, TurnLeft, TurnRight, Stop.
Reward and training: +10 on success, +0.25 for reducing Manhattan distance, -0.01 per step; PPO with Adam, lr 2.5e-4, 500-step horizon; 40M steps on Replica and 60M on Matterport3D.
Moving target: as in CMHM, the source picks random destinations, follows the shortest path, and moves with probability 0.3 per step.
Design choice: attention is applied over the feature dimension only, not over time, because temporal attention is unstable under partial observability and sample-hungry.

setting.backbone: Small CNN encoders + FSA + bidirectional GRU + actor-critic (trained from scratch with PPO)
setting.training_data: RL from scratch in SoundSpaces on Replica (40M steps) and Matterport3D (60M steps); sound splits: telephone, multiple heard (102 sounds), multiple unheard (73/11/18 train/val/test)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB and/or depth (128x128, 90° FoV) + binaural audio spectrogram
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: MoveForward, TurnLeft, TurnRight, Stop on a hidden navigability graph
setting.privileged: none at test time (reward shaping uses distance during training only)

numbers.extra: Replica; all 102 sounds heard in train/val/test
Replica; unheard sounds at test (73/11/18 split)

numbers_note: Results are in a custom moving-sound benchmark (SoundSpaces on Replica and Matterport3D), so 'bench' uses an 'other:' label; the split name 'test' is assumed because the paper does not name the split. Only the depth+audio main variant is listed; RGB, RGBD and blind variants are in Table 2 and the appendix tables.
results: With depth+audio, FSAAVN beats concat SoundSpaces, EMul, EM, CMHM and AV-WaN on SPLT/SSPLT/SRT in all six dataset/sound settings. For example, on Replica telephone SRT is 0.925 vs 0.892 for SoundSpaces, and on Matterport3D telephone SPLT is 0.520 vs 0.454. CMHM and AV-WaN are far behind, especially on Matterport3D.
limitations: Absolute performance on unheard sounds is low (SRT 0.358 on Replica, 0.391 on Matterport3D).
FSA gives no gain, and is sometimes worse, when there is no visual input (blind).
The moving target is a simple scripted agent (0.3 move probability, random destinations), and results come only from simulation with no real robot.
